To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the effectiveness of Chk1 inhibitors in killing cells is not due to excess firing of replication origins.

the effectiveness of checkpoint kinase inhibition at killing cancer cells depends only marginally on origin deregulation and that the accumulation of replication forks that cannot bypass replication barriers contributes to cell death independently of their speed.

(1) Chk1 inhibition causes the formation of replication barriers that compromise replication fork progression and cell survival independently of origin firing; (2) replication barrier formation depends on Chk1‐dependent CDK phosphorylation of Polη; and (3) replication barrier formation contributes to the sensitivity of cancer cells to Chk1 inhibitors.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how cells deal with replication barriers and the consequences of their accumulation.
the mechanisms of cell cycle control and DNA repair.
understanding the molecular basis of Chk1 inhibitor efficacy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Chk1 loss creates barriers that are bypassed by Polη and that compromise cell survival.
Chk1‐dependent replication barriers are a key determinant of the sensitivity of cancer cells to Chk1 inhibitors.
Chk1 inhibition does not only lead to an increased firing of origins, but it also causes the accumulation of replication forks that are slowed down and stalled by replication barriers.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the effectiveness of checkpoint kinase inhibitors in killing cancer cells is not only dependent on the effect they have on DNA replication initiation, but also on the accumulation of replication stress‐induced replication barriers.
Chk1‐dependent phosphorylation is required to ensure efficient replication barrier bypass, and that this is a key factor in the sensitivity of cancer cells to Chk1 inhibitors.

Chk1 inhibition does not only lead to the accumulation of DNA lesions but also to the accumulation of replication intermediates that are difficult to replicate, and that these two events contribute independently to cell death in Chk1 deficient cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that

Chk1‐dependent phosphorylation is not only a means to control replication origin firing, but also a mechanism to prevent the accumulation of replication intermediates that compromise the viability of cancer cells.
the effectiveness of Chk1 inhibitors in cancer cells depends on the accumulation of replication forks that stall at replication barriers.
the effectiveness of checkpoint kinase inhibitors is not only due to the inhibition of DNA replication initiation but also depends on their ability to remove replication barriers.
